content:
These past few months there's been a sharp decrease in the quality of the average new contributor's PR. These PRs will be hundreds or thousands of lines long while proving a comparatively simple result, or they'll be filled with dubious definitions and only their trivial consequences. The effort that it takes to fix them is comparable to the effort it takes to re-do things from scratch.

I don't want to name names, but I'd imagine most maintainers have come across multiple of these PRs as of late. What's to be done about them? Should they be left unreviewed to accrue dust until they inevitably fall off the queue? Should they be brought to the maintainers' attention so they can deal with them accordingly? Should we leave some standard message like "this PR doesn't meet our quality standards, see here"? I'm worried about potentially shooing away a new contributor, but I'm also worried about the queue becoming filled with increasingly sloppy material.

Violeta Hernández said:

These PRs will be hundreds of thousands of lines long

Just thousands, not hundreds of thousands. I feel that such PRs should be closed on sight, explaining that the new contributor must tighten their standards
I meant hundreds or thousands, not hundreds of thousands! Thankfully we haven't seen that just yet.
This must have been the same for many open source projects recently. How do other projects deal with this?
Fluxer is an open-source chat client closely modelled after Discord. Its guidelines for those who want to contribute with LLMs mandate that a human-written explanation accompany each PR
"Contributor must thoroughly understand what they're adding to the project"
Could the generality and broadness of something like mathlib / what it is trying to accomplish make such PRs more voluminous, in comparison to other "narrower" repositories?

Since it is "cheap" (in terms of the blood, sweat, and tears that the PR author needs to invest) to create such a PR, I think there has to be a much higher burden of proof that the code is useful, robust, maintainable, high quality.

One way to establish that is by showing:

  • that this code has been sitting in the ForMathlib/ folder of downstream repo XyzzyTheory
  • was refactored and generalized i times in the past
  • but now has been stable for k time (k > 2 months??)
  • and has N declarations depending on it, with a DAG depth of d (maybe N > 400 and d > 10)

If

  • I know something about Xyzzy theory, and
  • I recognize the theorems that are being developed in the XyzyyTheory repo, and
  • the blueprint is passing snif tests,
    then I might be quite inclined to believe that moving (without refactoring!) this piece of code from ForMathlib/ into Mathlib proper is a worthwhile thing, and the code has proven itself to be worth its LOC in gold.

This is a higher standard than we apply today to human contributions.
If your AI complains about that, then I'm inclined to tell it

:shrug: C'est la vie. Deal with it.

Ok, that was a bit provocative. But I'm trying to work out whether we can find some pragmatic and deterministic measures of high-quality code. The above is an attempt to have a measurable way of determining that code is useful in/for the broader ecosystem.
And then hope you don't get a hit piece published about you, I guess

Perhaps one possible approach is a policy that your first 10/20/N PRs must be entirely handwritten. After that, you can be said to have a passable enough understanding of mathlib style to decide on appropriate use of AI. At a minimum we know that you _actually know some Lean_. This requires honesty from reviewees but for the moment it’s not hard to spot AI proofs
Or put length limits on first PRs? I think that might even be good for completely human-written contributions?
I like both Vlad's and Thomas' suggestions. (Though I bet some would object to the first requirement.)
I would be more inclined to implement the minimum PR requirement than the length limit. I'd put the floor at 5 PRs

I like the length limit idea (although this can vary depending on how git actually evaluates diffs which is heuristic).

In addition, I think maybe it is a good idea to institute an "approved PR" badge. One gets this badge for their PR by proposing a PR in a dedicated zulip channel and explaining it succinctly (without sounding like an LLM). Maybe they also submit a draft PR. Maintainers can skim it and give a badge of approval. For example maintainers could tell the contributor to shorten the PR or focus on something specific. Only PRs with the approved badge are accepted from contributors with less than 10 or 20 merged PRs.

Right now, new contributors' contributions are often implicitly approved (by virtue of being mentored by experienced community members). For those PRs, adding another hoop to jump through feels not great. (Mathlib's PR process is intimidating enough already.)

I'd rather make it easier to quickly close slop PRs. We're seeing an increase of new members on zulip posting about AI-powered formalisation - so getting better at directing their enthusiasm in useful ways would help more.

I think Michael has a good point. Certain regulations can have an asymmetric affect on well meaning newcomers versus bad actors.

It seems Violeta's original question about a standardized message for these cases could be useful for a standard route to quickly closing these PRs. (Maybe it also triggers a queue tag for AI PRs to close??)

Shreyas Srinivas said:

In addition, I think maybe it is a good idea to institute an "approved PR" badge. One gets this badge for their PR by proposing a PR in a dedicated zulip channel and explaining it succinctly (without sounding like an LLM).

Instead of an “approved PR” label for all new contributors, would it make sense to flip this and label LLM-generated PRs with an LLM label? (Or uses-LLM, LLM-assisted?) Then when LLM and new-contributor appear together, we know how to gently suggest better ways to start contributing.

It could be taken as a bit of a scarlet letter, but maybe that’s just the value-neutral cost of making review take more time? :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes: We do want LLM use to be declared explicitly anyway.

Perhaps (only) LLM PRs specifically could then receive an additional label (attached by reviewers/maintainers) showing the PR authors are attempting to meet some standards we put in place for high-quality contributions in good-faith. (human-curated?)

I have a tangential question here. Are there any good ways to identify LLM generated code? While reviewing I often see some highly suboptimal use of tactics and lemmas that looks suspicious but to me it might as well be a novice monkey-typing random tactics that they know until Lean said yes. (I also did this when I started, and frankly I still do it now at times, and it is just that my experience gives me a fairly good random distribution that usually make things work nicely). Also another telltale sign is having weird comments like

/— Let a be a natural number with the value 3 -/
def a : Nat := 3

But it might as well be some novice who genuinely have no idea what’s going on without the comments or mistakenly thought that comments are required at every step of proofs. I do not want to mistakenly accuse people (especially newcomers) of LLM slop but I fear I might be wasting my reviewing energy otherwise.

LLM-generated Lean code usually comes with an LLM-generated PR description (and the reverse is also true), which is usually easy to identify. Use of any markdown headings is a pretty good indicator. (excluding the --- in PR descriptions which sometimes creates accidental headings)

Making some thoughts a bit more concrete, here's a proposal for what the overall flow of social actions/responsibilities/expectations could look like.

Note: the goal of this proposal is to smooth out the "what do I do about this" problem reviewers face when encountering an LLM PR, while letting us both encourage good code and more easily close PRs that are not meeting the standards. (It's kind of a wrapper around our standards for LLM code, so we can decouple the social part of this problem.)

  • triage: LLM PRs are identified and LLM label is added.
    • PR authors are encouraged to add LLM label themselves by commenting LLM
    • reviewers suspecting an LLM PR should
      • gently ask the author if there's any doubt (maybe we could have a template for doing this to help reviewers)
      • add the label if there is no doubt
      • in all cases comment encouraging PR author to do so themselves
  • then, when LLM label is applied to PRs, we communicate of expectations and extend trust (or not):
    • a bot comments on LLM-labeled PRs and points to [LLM Contribution Responsibilities]
      • if new-contributor is present as well, the bot also points to [Different ways to start contributing]
      • if PR author has several LLM-labeled PRs already merged, the bot auto-applies human-curated label—i.e. the PR author is a trusted LLM user, and this saves some further reviewer triage (note: bot should still comment with [LLM Contribution Responsibilities] in this case to give reviewers quick access to the standards)
      • if PR is over the length limit and does not have human-curated, the bot also applies awaiting-author and explains the length limit requirement
    • reviewers then further triage PRs with (only) the LLM label:
      • if the author is acting in good faith/working to meet the responsibilties, apply human-curated label (does not have to yet fully meet the high standards, the author just has to show that they are definitely acting in good faith to do so)
      • if not (e.g. it's been a while since the bot has commented about [LLM Contribution Responsibilities] and there is still no movement in that direction from the PR author)
        • comment to please meet the [LLM Contribution Responsibilities] and apply awaiting-author
          • if awaiting-author has been removed by the author without material good-faith effort to meet the responsibilities, close the PR with a stock comment that the responsibilities haven't been fulfilled and standards are high for LLM PRs, and review time is at a premium. new-contributors are told future contributions are welcome.

This is of course just a proposal to iterate on, so I've made some specific choices :)

This is a bit outside the proposal per se, but I think the [LLM Contribution Responsibilities] document/blurb that this process wraps should (at least) include the responsibilities of:

  • asking the contributor to lay out the "here is why this is good code" evidence Johan mentioned in the PR description (or in a comment)
  • meeting a length limit
  • meeting high quality standards, with examples of what LLMs frequently get wrong

and should include

  • clear communication/warning about what happens if you don't try to meet these responsibilities, i.e. that your PR may be closed promptly
  • why these standards are necessary: short explanation about review time, etc. :)

Likewise the [Different ways to start contributing] document/blurb should explain why we want new contributors to contribute differently, in a welcoming way: it builds trust with the contributor and helps the contributor familiarize themselves with code standards that LLMs struggle to meet. Communicate also that LLM users are expected to closely pilot LLM contributions, and familiarization with ordinary contribution saves a lot of review time.

It should also perhaps(?) gently suggest converting LLM PRs to draft PRs until the contributor is no longer a new-contributor.

I was annoyed enough by some bad LLM-written PRs that I created a label LLM-generated (renaming welcome!) and tried to label most PRs as such. (I will have missed some; I was not always exhaustive about backfilling closed PRs. Be my guest to change this!) I suggest that we label new PRs this way, to expose this information in a better way.
I like the above proposal a lot and think it would be a great forward. I don't have time right now to push this myself, though.
Should a bot respond with a standard message and close?
To every LLM-generated PR? That would affect nearly all of Kim's recent PRs and some of yours, so I guess you mean something different :-)

Aah, I thought you only intended this for

Michael Rothgang said:

some bad LLM-written PRs
Oh yes, a bot closing these would be welcome!
But then we need to reserve the label for only such bad PRs
So maybe LLM-slop instead of LLM-generated?
Should we request the author of the PR to tag LLM-generated when it is?
We are already asking for disclosure. We could be a bit more precise about the how, indeed.

In my opinion, there's room for both

  • LLM (or LLM-generated), which is purely informational and fairly objective (with lots of grey area, of course), and
  • LLM-slop which could trigger a bot commenting with a standard message and auto-closing.

Would it be preferable to pick a more neutral term than "slop" for the latter label? While I agree completely with the action of quickly closing there is still (hopefully...) a human on the other side of the PR that is in the most charitable interpretation a newcomer unfamiliar with Mathlib standards.

I strongly recommend 

LLM-lq

for LLM-low-quality. It's better to be seen as snobbish because of upholding high-standards then snobbish because you think you're upholding high standards and being insulting about it.

content: Maybe use low-quality , because I would struggle disambiguating LLM-lq if I saw it suddenly. That being said , this may prompt the contributor to try use LLM more aggressively to increase the quality somehow. The underlying issue is often too much lack of comprehension and thus inability to adapt the code.
LLM-missing-QA/LLM-without-QA (quality assurance)?

LLM slop is burning out maintainers in open source, at relatively large scale. (A recent Rust survey lists this as the largest risk factor for maintainer burnout, for instance.) It is taking a drain on mathlib maintainers already. (Let me just say that staying friendly in the face of our deluge of slop is hard work.) This is not sustainable.
Regarding concrete suggestions, perhaps "LLM-burdensome", "LLM-maintainance-burden" (or simply "burdensome") would do.

The underlying issue is often too much lack of comprehension and thus inability to adapt the code.

Strong agreement here. I generally love to mentor contributors who want to learn, even if they don't come back. But that requires the human willing to learn themselves, and understanding what they do. "More LLM" in the absence of that understanding is fruitless, a waste of time (which is scarce already) and frankly, rather disrespectful of the maintance efforts.
Do we need a label if we're just going to close those immediately? Or do we want to track statistics or something?
The idea was "the label triggers a bot which auto-closes with a comment".
(And I am always curious about statistics; that might be me.)

Michael Rothgang said:

Regarding concrete suggestions, perhaps "LLM-burdensome", "LLM-maintainance-burden" (or simply "burdensome") would do.

I agree with Chris Henson that a more neutral tag is preferred. Ideally, a tag that would inspire the submitter to do better work is what is wanted. Rather than burdensome, a suggestion of "needs work" would do. I don't expect the LLMs (this month) to do better, but perhaps pointing to a posting of a bad example versus a good example would do more to alleviate the problem? (Perhaps inspire the submitter to look at their own example?)

content:
Michael Rothgang said:

LLM slop is burning out maintainers in open source, at relatively large scale. (A recent Rust survey lists this as the largest risk factor for maintainer burnout, for instance.) It is taking a drain on mathlib maintainers already. (Let me just say that staying friendly in the face of our deluge of slop is hard work.) This is not sustainable.

I want to clarify that I'm not disagreeing with this at all. In my personal experience in CSLib, which has orders of magnitude less scale than Mathlib, it is already a factor that I personally find quite distasteful and exhausting. We have even had one extreme case where I closed an obviously slop PR and received a very aggressive and vulgar response in return (that was promptly handled by the Zulip moderators). This is part of part of why I think a standardized message/label is a good idea, in placing some distance between the person closing the PR.

Despite all this I think it is worth trying to be as empathetic as possible to the more well-intentioned cases if it is as simple as picking different verbiage. For them, it may be their first time interacting with open source at all and they may have little context of the maintainer perspective.

It seems very important to me that no single reviewer can be singled out for the decision to close an LLM-generated PR. In particular, the process should not be to add a label to the PR, because the information of who added the label is public.

I suppose a practical solution there might be mentioning the PR in a dedicated channel in the reviewers stream, and a bot taking it all from there (adding a label and, perhaps after a grace period, closing)

This is likely a completely blunt tool so just spit balling , but would making new contributors do one PR at a time (just for those first ones) help with the issue? I also notice some people submitting multiple PRs that sit open since they are too LLM for anyone to dare, and then potentially continuing to open more LLM content.

Does anyone have any visibility off the top of their heads, as to whether new contributor PRs are often AI nowadays, and if there are many new contributors opening multiple LLM PRs(also not sure how this would be practically implemented if its even possible)?
Are my PRs slop because I have quite a few of them open?
You are not a new contributor.
how about LLM-needs-work for "bad ones" and LLM-assisted for "good ones"

Yaël Dillies said:

It seems very important to me that no single reviewer can be singled out for the decision to close an LLM-generated PR. In particular, the process should not be to add a label to the PR, because the information of who added the label is public.

I don't understand why you want this? Reviews themselves are not anonymous either?
I also think it's important to be able to discuss decisions and ask for a second opinion...
So perhaps the solution to the problem (which I don't understand yet) is that instead we need two reviewers to discuss and agree to place the label?
I guess it is about this.

We don't want to inspire abuse directed at those reviewers; this has happened in the past. (Those comments often take place in DMs or are promptly deleted, which is why they are not publically visible.)

Edward van de Meent said:

I also think it's important to be able to discuss decisions and ask for a second opinion...

Agreed. That's not going away, though: discussing a PR in public is fine (the cases discussed here are the clear-cut ones!). If need be, there is a non-public reviewers stream. (Most PR reviews happen in public, that is good and should stay this way.)

One question about LLM-needs-work: to me this implies that we want the contributor to work more on their PR and resubmit, and believe there is a long-term interest of adding the content to Mathlib, whilst I am not sure it is always the case. How about LLM-does-not-comply, together with a message saying it does not comply with the community standards?

Michael Rothgang said:

Edward van de Meent said:

I also think it's important to be able to discuss decisions and ask for a second opinion...

Agreed. That's not going away, though: discussing a PR in public is fine (the cases discussed here are the clear-cut ones!). If need be, there is a non-public reviewers stream. (Most PR reviews happen in public, that is good and should stay this way.)

My meaning of that quote is from the perspective of the PR author...
And if you anonymize review decisions, you're asking the author to discuss those decisions with a wall
I think we might need a mix of both. Depending on whether situations are good-faith or bad-faith.
For context, we are currently "fighting" a user who has created ~15 sockpuppets and is constantly posting the same slop. In such cases, putting up a wall is good.

Laura Monk said:

Should we request the author of the PR to tag LLM-generated when it is?

It might have been a bit premature, but I decided to be a bit proactive and self-tag one of my PRs (#36765) as LLM-generated. It turns out the tagging bot did not respond. I guess this is because the tag is not in the set of allowed tags for mere contributors? If there is consensus on using this tag already, I figure it should be enabled. This seems like an easier question to agree on than the "slop" tag.

How about the inverse approach: Every new-contributor PR will be automatically closed if it is not endorsed by a "trusted community member" in the first 24 hours after creation. Until then, the PR is tagged as awaiting-endorsement and does not appear on the queue. Furthermore, any contributor may not have two PRs awaiting-endorsement at the same time, if they open more they will be immediately closed.

"Trusted community member" of course needs a definition. It could for example be "mathlib contributor with at least n-commits in the last m-months".
That seems unnecessarily aggressive towards legitimate new contributors. I certainly wouldn't come back to a project that did that to me
I think that would also lead to cries on Zulip of "please endorse my PR!" (we already get arXiv endorsement requests, which is only tangentially related)

I believe the current review process is already aggressive, this doesn't change much.... The only question is, do we need those "cheap" contributions?
I my opinion, if it doesn't cause to much stress on CI, we may consider reviewing only one of them at a time? This doesn't seem consuming to much resource and enabling new contributers to learn properly (:

Nailin Guan said:

the current review process is already aggressive

Can you expand on this? I'm not sure what you mean.

Nevermind, I didn't express it clear, I mean the reviewing already need new contributers to admit great shift in habit and aspect, I think this endorse issue (or some other kind just for example) wouldn't be considered too aggresive if somebody know how review process is working.

It looks like since 2 days ago some LLM-generated PRs were closed with a message about LLM quality. AFAICT this is not automated, a human (reviewer or above?) manually DMs a bot asking to close a PR, and then the bot closes it anonymously.
There was also some pushback here.
I assume this was discussed in reviewer channels, but is there anything you can share publicly about the discussion that lead to this decision? The reasons for wanting it are clear, but I'm interested in what changed recently: did people change their opinions? or was there a giant wave of AI PRs? Is there an announcement planned? Are you holding a vote per PR or is it single-handed?
(btw I'm not opposed to it, I like that the title of this thread now has an answer, cool stuff)

Indeed reviewers and maintainers have decided to close a substantial amount of PRs that use LLM generated code.  When a new contributor makes a PR, the code quality is often far from Mathlib standards, which is completely normal. This means that reviewing such a PR takes A LOT of time. Between recommendations and comments about mathematical relevance, mathematical generality, location of the new declarations, and above all the remarks concerning the code style (use of tactics, many golfs, more idiomatic statements, use of already existing API etc.), it is not rare in my personal experience that a review on such a PR requires a comment every two line or so. As I said, this is completely normal, we were all beginners once and this review process is one of the best way to learn about Mathlib conventions and various ways to write lean more efficiently. Reviewers and maintainers are well aware of that, and this is why they put a lot of time in reviewing these PRs (and many of them do that besides their everyday job). They are also aware that this is some kind of investment: by taking this time now, they not only teach the contributor, which is already a great thing, but they also ensure that the future PRs the contributor may open will be of better quality, so that they can become a regular contributor to the library, which will in the end be good for the library. Once they get more used to Mathlib conventions, they may even start to do reviews on their own for new contributors, teaching them about Mathlib conventions etc.

Turn now to LLM-generated PR. The code in such a PR is most of the time of low quality, at best it is the same as an average new contributor. Thus it requires at least the same time investment described above from reviewers and maintainers. However, since the contributor does not write the code themselves, they do not learn in the process, which means that all the benefits previously described do not happen (and I am not even talking about PRs where even the messages from the contributor are LLM generated). Adding the fact that this kind of PR is generally quite long (i.e. more than 100 lines, which is not that much for a regular PR but in that case there are lots of comments to be made so it is), and more and more of them appear, the maintainers and reviewers have decided that it was not worth spending time reviewing these PRs, and started to close several of them.

Regarding the system, indeed the maintainer or reviewer who wants to close a PR will ask a bot to do it, so that the name of the person who closes the PR is not public (it is available for maintainers and reviewers though). This is to avoid any kind of backlash as happened in the case of matplotlib, where a maintainer was publicly attacked by an AI agent after closing a PR.

Regarding the closing message, it was not generated by an LLM. The goal was to explain in a brief way what I wrote above. This avoids every maintainer or reviewer who wants to close a PR to have to think about how to phrase the issue we are all aware of, which again is time that is not well spent.

Let me add pieces of context:

  • about decision making: this policy was decided by the reviewers and maintainers. Decisions are generally made by consensus: we aim for a solution everybody in the group supports, and there being no objection.
  • as additional context, LLM-generated (posts about) slop and PRs can burn out reviewers and maintainers very quickly. Reviewer time is essential to mathlib's success. This is an issue already, it's just barely visible on zulip because "slop" messages are usually moderated quickly.
Thank you for doing this! I believe it benefits us all, including non-(reviewers/maintainers).
See #General announcements > PSA: mathlib AI policy for mathlib's official AI policy.

For comparison, arXiv uses a double “registration” and “endorsement” strategy. Even when you wish to publish in a new category, you might need endorsement if you haven't submitted papers in the recent years. Moreover, arXiv is implementing (or considers implementing) a permanent ban of authors who submit completely AI-generated material. See https://bsky.app/profile/aniloza.bsky.social/post/3mltoq2cnhc2u

arXiv drama the last few days has been crazy. It is funny (and sad) to see the amount of people who think it is their god-given right to post on arXiv.

I think arXiv has a good system, but it is a fair critique to say that arXiv is not "open source" in the same way as Mathlib. Their system is intended to prioritize papers from well-known, respected research institutions—not submissions from the general public. That means sometimes scientists from private sector or unknown universities, especially in the third world, can be left out.
I think open source is the wrong word here: you can have a piece of open source software that does not allow external PRs. That is totally fine, no project has to accept contributions.
You're right. I meant to say open collaboration.

p.s. One think that might also be worth trying is to actually involve LLM's on the review side, especially if the pr is largely LLM generated. Writing high quality code is much more difficult task than recognizing high quality code, in the same way it is much easier to recognize if someone is singing beautifully compared to trying to sing yourself. So point an LLM to some example PR's where people have given particular feedback on what is bad code and why. Point it to some PR's that have good code. Let it summarise what makes code good or bad according to mathlib standards. In this way the human cost of dealing with slop PR's can also be significantly reduced.
Of course, one needs to be careful with this with non LLM generated PR's, since you don't want to put a lot of burden on human devs in order to deal with LLM generated reviews.
This idea has been considered before (search zulip for "botbaki", for instance). Right now, the comments are of mixed quality (and do not replace proper review).
